characteristics.roast: Light or none (in green style); traditional style has medium roast

description.short: Tightly rolled ball-shaped oolong with a milky-orchid aroma and light oxidation
description.overview: One of China's most recognizable oolongs, rolled into dense pellets. The modern style (since the 1990s) emphasizes freshness and floral notes over heavy roasting.
description.leaf: Dense dark-green rolled pellets that unfurl into whole leaves upon brewing
description.aroma: Orchid, fresh cream, subtle floral trail
description.taste: Smooth, creamy-floral flavor with delicate sweetness and minimal astringency
description.aftertaste: Fresh, floral, lingering for several minutes in the mouth ("hui gan")
description.processing: Harvesting → withering → tossing/shaking to bruise leaf edges for partial oxidation → fixation (kill-green) → repeated cloth-wrapped rolling into pearls/balls → drying

history.origin: The name means "Iron Goddess of Mercy" — according to legend, an impoverished farmer tended a dilapidated shrine to Guanyin, the goddess of mercy, and in a dream she guided him to a miraculous tea bush behind the temple.
history.development: Cultivated in Anxi County since at least the 18th century; for generations it was produced in a traditional, higher-oxidized, and charcoal-roasted style.
history.modern: In the 1990s, Anxi producers shifted toward lighter oxidation influenced by Taiwan and Southeast Asian market preferences, resulting in the contemporary fragrant, greener style.
interestingFacts: Authentic old Tie Guan Yin bushes grow slowly with low yields, so most commercial tea today comes from higher-yielding clones.
The name has become synonymous with an entire style of rolled oolong, even when produced outside Anxi.
